titre: A Statement on Race, Corrected Within a Year
accroche: In 1950, UNESCO wrote that race is a “social myth” more than a biological phenomenon. A year later, a second committee took the text up again.
contenu_vulgarise:
In December 1949, UNESCO brought together eight experts from several countries, mostly social scientists, among them Claude Lévi-Strauss. The anthropologist Ashley Montagu was appointed rapporteur: after criticism from several scientists who were consulted, he is the one who revised the final text. Published on July 18, 1950, it stated that mental capacities are similar across human groups, that no evidence shows biological degeneration from the mixing of populations, and that no correlation exists between a nation or a religion and any given race. Its most discussed sentence goes further: race is described there as being less a biological phenomenon than a “social myth,” and the text adds that biological studies support the ethic of “universal brotherhood” among men.

## A Statement Sharply Criticized

The text aimed at a clear goal: to answer the racial theories of Nazism, five years after the regime's fall. But the statement drew sharp criticism. Cyril Darlington, Ronald Fisher, and Ruggles Gates, among others, challenged it, and even scientists rather sympathetic to its antiracism found the claim of a “universal brotherhood” resting on biology weak. According to Encyclopedia.com, exaggerated assertions lacking scientific backing damaged the text's effectiveness; the original committee consisted mostly of social scientists, with Montagu the only physical anthropologist.

Under pressure, UNESCO then assembled a second committee, made up of geneticists and physical anthropologists, with Leslie Clarence Dunn as rapporteur; Montagu sat on it too, and the new text was presented as an explanation of the first rather than a revision. Before publishing, the organization sent the draft to ninety-six scientists for comment. The text that emerged, in June 1951, was more tentative: it did not carry over the idea that biology would prove universal brotherhood, and recognized that many populations can be classified in racial terms by anthropologists, while admitting that the process of differentiation remains unknown.

## Two Statements, Not One

The episode is often told as though science had, once and for all, delivered its verdict on race in 1950. The reality is more awkward for anyone looking for a single authority: the more assertive version was sharply criticized by other scientists, and the one that succeeded it, a year later, did not carry over the idea of universal brotherhood, after a consultation of ninety-six specialists. This proves neither that the first was right and the second wrong, nor the reverse. It proves that the line between a biological fact and a social category was never settled by a single stroke, even one signed by eight experts seated in the same room. It was debated, through successive committees, between disciplines that do not measure scientific caution the same way.

repere.texte: Before publishing its 1951 version, UNESCO sent the second committee's draft to ninety-six scientists for comment.

carte.punch: A UNESCO statement on race, sharply criticized, then reworked within a year.
carte.idee: In July 1950, UNESCO wrote that race is a social myth more than a biological phenomenon. Scholars challenged the statement; a second committee of geneticists and physical anthropologists published a more tentative version in 1951.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Montagu's part in UNESCO's committee of experts on race, and the controversies that followed the 1950 statement.

quiz.question: Why does UNESCO publish a second statement on race as early as 1951, a year after the first?
choix: Because the French government refuses to distribute the 1950 text in its schools
Because the criticism of the 1950 text pushes UNESCO to convene a second committee
Because Ashley Montagu resigns from the committee before the work is finished
Because the United Nations demands a shorter version of the original text
quiz.explication: The 1950 text held that race was less a biological phenomenon than a social myth; major critics, including Darlington, Fisher, and Gates, followed. Under pressure, UNESCO convened a second committee of geneticists and physical anthropologists, whose 1951 version is more tentative.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who revises the final text of the 1950 statement, as the committee's rapporteur?
choix: The scientist Ronald Fisher, one of the text's critics
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Ashley Montagu, whom the Encyclopedia.com overview presents as the only physical anthropologist on the 1949 committee, is appointed its rapporteur and revises the text published in July 1950. Dunn will be the rapporteur of the second committee, in 1951; Lévi-Strauss sat on the first committee without being its rapporteur.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 1951 statement withdraw compared with the 1950 one?
choix: Any mention of Ashley Montagu's work
The entire 1950 text, replaced wholesale with nothing in common
The claim that biology would prove a “universal brotherhood” among men
The publication date, pushed back a year
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1951 version does not carry over the claim that biology would support universal brotherhood; Montagu nonetheless sits on the second committee, presented as an explanation of the first.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before publishing the 1951 version, what does UNESCO do with the second committee's draft?
choix: It holds a public vote in member states
It sends the draft to ninety-six scientists for comment
It has the text translated into a hundred languages before publication
It asks for the approval of the United States government
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The draft is sent to ninety-six scientists for comment before the June 1951 publication. The 1950 text had also been submitted to scientists in several countries before being finalized.
